intro: Ivan Ilić plays Debussy’s La cathédrale engloutie, where bare fifths become bells and a great C-major melody becomes an organ. The tune returns at the end as though heard through water.

sections.label: A · Fifths across the piano
sections.mNote: Widely spaced notes ring around the rising fifths

sections.label: A′ · Triplets out of the mist
sections.mNote: B-major chords rise over a rolling left hand

sections.label: B · C major fills the keyboard
sections.mNote: A low C supports the broad chordal melody

sections.label: C · The low chant returns
sections.mNote: C♯ minor carries an earlier phrase towards another crest

sections.label: B′ · The melody becomes an echo
sections.mNote: Soft C-major chords return above rocking quavers

cues.title: A fifth left open
cues.text: The first chord contains only G and D, spread across the keyboard. There is no third to make it major or minor. Rising fifths move through the middle of the piano while the outer notes hang in the air, like bells heard across water.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Préludes I, no. 10, bars 1–6; Piano Practical Editions, Centenary Edition (2018), p. 67. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/42/IMSLP881620-PMLP2394-Preludes_book_1_.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets stir below
cues.text: B major brings sharps into the rising chords. The left hand rolls in triplets beneath them, moving more continuously than the opening bells. Debussy’s marking describes a slow emergence from the mist; the piano grows towards an organ’s full voice.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 16–27, Centenary Edition, p. 68: B-major passage, left-hand triplets and Peu à peu sortant de la brume.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano becomes an organ
cues.text: G dominant-seventh harmony prepares a broad C-major statement. Both hands carry the tune in thick parallel chords above a low C. The marking asks for a sonorous sound without harshness: a full organ, with the bass held beneath its moving voices.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 22–41, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: dominant preparation, low C and Sonore sans dureté at the chordal statement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chant starts again
cues.text: The great chords retreat into isolated bell notes. A quieter chant returns in C♯ minor, low in the piano, carrying a phrase already heard near the beginning. It gradually climbs and thickens until the hands fill the keyboard again.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 42–61, Centenary Edition, pp. 70–71: withdrawal, C♯-minor recall at bar 47 and expansion towards bar 61.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy at the piano
cues.text: On 25 May 1910, Debussy plays this prelude himself at a Société musicale indépendante concert in Paris. He presents it with three others from the first book: Danseuses de Delphes, Voiles and La danse de Puck.
cues.evidence: The work catalogue records Debussy’s performance of nos. 1, 2, 10 and 11 in Paris on 25 May 1910. https://imslp.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9ludes%2C_Livre_1%2C_CD_125_(Debussy%2C_Claude)

cues.title: The organ becomes an echo
cues.text: The C-major melody comes back lower and much softer. Quavers rock underneath it, marked floating and muffled; above them the chords sing the old tune as an echo. At the close, the rocking stops and the opening’s fifths ring once more.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 72–89, Centenary Edition, pp. 71–72: Comme un écho de la phrase entendue précédemment, flottant et sourd and the final return of rising fifths.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A semitone sets the bass moving
transitions.to: A′ · Triplets out of the mist
transitions.how: The bass drops from C to B. The right hand keeps its rising chords, now in B major, while left-hand triplets fill the spaces beneath them. Debussy marks the piano as gradually coming out of the mist.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 14–19, Centenary Edition, pp. 67–68: bass C–B, B-major chords and triplets.

transitions.title: G opens the door to C
transitions.from: A′ · Triplets out of the mist
transitions.to: B · C major fills the keyboard
transitions.how: The ascent passes through E♭ major and reaches G dominant-seventh harmony. The triplets fall away. A low C then supports the broad melody in parallel chords, fortissimo, with the tune doubled through both hands.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 19–28, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: E♭-major passage, G dominant seventh and C-major statement.

transitions.title: Bell notes uncover the chant
transitions.from: B · C major fills the keyboard
transitions.how: The C-major chords soften into widely spaced bell notes. The bass settles beneath a low C♯-minor chant, marked Un peu moins lent. Its phrase recalls the opening pages and begins to climb again.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 42–53, Centenary Edition, p. 70: bell notes, C♯-minor recall and Un peu moins lent.

transitions.title: The full chords return underwater
transitions.to: B′ · The melody becomes an echo
transitions.how: Parallel seventh chords descend from the second crest. A low rocking figure begins beneath them, and the C-major tune returns pianissimo above it. Debussy lowers the chordal melody on the keyboard and calls it an echo.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 61–75, Centenary Edition, p. 71: parallel seventh chords, low quavers and the quiet C-major echo.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
